content: A cervical stitch, also known as cerclage, is a medical procedure used to prevent preterm deliveries in women who have experienced pregnancy losses in the second trimester or have other risk factors, such as a short cervix identified through digital or ultrasound examination. The procedure can be performed prophylactically, before the cervix begins to dilate, or as an emergency measure when the cervix has already started to shorten and dilate, with the aim of halting labor. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic and emergency cerclage, as well as to determine whether any specific technique of stitch insertion is superior to others. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (up to July 2002 and updated in November 2009), proceedings from international and European society meetings on feto-maternal medicine, recurrent miscarriage, and reproductive medicine, and direct contact with researchers in the field. The review included all randomized trials comparing cervical cerclage with expectant management or no cerclage during pregnancy, as well as trials comparing different cerclage techniques or other interventions. Quasi-randomized trials were excluded. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. When necessary, additional clarification was sought from the authors of the trials. Results were reported as relative risks using either fixed or random effects models. The analysis included six trials involving a total of 2,175 women. Four trials compared prophylactic cerclage with no cerclage. Overall, there was no significant reduction in pregnancy loss or preterm delivery rates. However, the largest trial demonstrated a modest reduction in births occurring before 33 weeks of gestation (relative risk 0.75, 95% confidence interval 0.58 to 0.98). Cervical cerclage was associated with mild fever, increased use of tocolytic therapy, and higher rates of hospital admission, but no serious morbidity was reported. Two trials investigated the use of therapeutic cerclage in women with a short cervix identified on ultrasound. The pooled results did not show a significant reduction in total pregnancy loss, early pregnancy loss, or preterm delivery before 28 and 34 weeks of gestation in women who underwent cervical cerclage. The authors concluded that cervical cerclage should not be routinely offered to women at low or medium risk of mid-trimester pregnancy loss, regardless of cervical length as measured by ultrasound. The role of cervical cerclage in women with a short cervix remains uncertain due to the limited number of randomized participants, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. Additionally, there is no available information on the impact of cervical cerclage or its alternatives on the family unit or long-term outcomes. It is important to note that 23 citations in the awaiting classification section of the review may influence the conclusions once they are assessed.
